[877] Particular restraint will continue to be shown in military flights in national border areas. **2.3 The international background** **2.3.1 East/West relations** Since 1985, there have been clear tendencies for relaxation in the development of East/West relations, and the relationship between the superpowers has entered a more constructive phase

[878] Internal developments in the Soviet Union have contributed to this

[879] The American-Soviet summits in November 1985, October 1986, December 1987 and May/June 1988 have confirmed the great importance of superpower dialogue for the international climate

[880] The summits have also led to progress in ongoing negotiations on disarmament and arms control

[881] The most important concrete result so far has been the agreement to eliminate all US and Soviet land-based intermediate-range missiles on a global basis, an agreement that has been ratified by both parties

[882] The resumption of the top-level superpower dialogue has also been accompanied by an intensification and regularization of general political contacts between the United States and the Soviet Union

[883] This has led, among other things, to expanded cooperation in a number of fields

[884] The progress in the work towards nuclear disarmament has reinforced the importance of the disparities in conventional armaments

[885] This highlights the role and interest of European states in the military part of the détente process

[886] NATO and Warsaw Pact states are now discussing the mandate for new negotiations on conventional stability

[887] The military aspects of the CSCE process have taken on an increasingly important role with a view to increasing mutual security and confidence on the European continent

[888] The KNE negotiations that fall

[889] In 1986 resulted in the Stockholm Document, which is in this respect a milestone, in that the 35 CSCE states agreed on a number of concrete and binding confidence-building measures in connection with land-based military activity in Europe

[890] From the Western side, new negotiations are envisioned with the aim of further expanding the existing KNE regime

[891] At the same time, it is important that the non-military aspects of the CSCE process are not lost sight of

[892] Here, small and medium-sized European states have both vital interests to safeguard and opportunities to play a central role

[893] The Soviet Union's stance on human rights has shown some positive features, but remains a brake on the policy of détente

[894] The Soviet Union's unwillingness to adopt substantive and binding formulations in the area of human rights has so far been an obstacle to reaching a final document from the ongoing third CSCE follow-up meeting in Vienna

[895] Regarding the situation in Afghanistan, a framework agreement was signed in Geneva in April 1988 between Pakistan and Afghanistan, i.e. the communist regime in Kabul, which the Soviet Union and the United States support and act as guarantors for

[896] The framework agreement includes, among other things, the withdrawal of Soviet forces from Afghanistan, and further that the repatriation and settlement of Afghan refugees shall commence. Norway's participation in foreign, defense and security policy cooperation in Western Europe is linked to two bodies

[897] The Eurogroup in NATO and the Independent European Programme Group (IEPG

[898] In relation to the EC and the EC countries' foreign policy cooperation, European Political Cooperation, the result of the referendum in 1972 sets limits on Norway's ability to participate

[899] The EPS has mainly emerged since 1972, and from 1981 it has been officially recognized that this cooperation also encompasses the political and economic aspects of security policy

[900] The Western European Union (WEU), which consists of seven countries that are all EC and NATO members, has been in a revitalization process since

[901] The overall goal here is to create a suitable Western European forum for cooperation and coordination also for the purely military aspects of security policy

[902] Developments in Western Europe over the past 10-15 years have been influenced by the EC, both in the economic and foreign policy areas

[903] This trend has been reinforced in the last couple of years and is expected to be further strengthened

[904] With its 12 member states and approximately 320 million of Western Europe's 350 million inhabitants, the EC today stands as the undisputed center of gravity in European politics

[905] The expansion of the EC from 10 to 12 member states from January 1986 (Spain, Portugal) meant that the political centre of gravity in Europe was shifted southwards

[906] This could also have significant consequences for the Northern European states that are not members of the EC

[907] While the EU countries can be expected to want to further develop a comprehensive Mediterranean policy that also includes security policy considerations, the conditions are not similarly conducive to a comprehensive policy when it comes to Europe's northern flank

[908] The Single European Act of 1985 established European foreign policy cooperation (EPC) as a treaty

[909] The aim is to achieve a European foreign policy that coordinates both national and community foreign policy behavior

[910] The original distinction between the EC and the EPS has been abolished

[911] The European Commission thus participates in the EPS as a full partner

[912] Security policy is dealt with in a separate paragraph in the Single European Act, but is limited to the political and economic aspects

[913] However, it may prove difficult to separate the different aspects of security policy from each other

[914] Consultations on the CSCE are included as a permanent part of the EPS, despite the fact that arms control and confidence-building measures also have a clear military side

[915] There are, however, limits to how far the EPS can go in developing security policy cooperation further, partly due to Ireland's neutral status and the restrictive attitude towards such cooperation from the Danish and Greek sides

[916] From January 1987, a small EPS secretariat was established in Brussels, among other things to ensure continuity and follow-up of EPS decisions

[917] It is too early to say what real impact the secretariat will have, but it must be assumed that it will contribute to increasing the importance of the EPS as a factor in international politics

[918] The increasing foreign policy cooperation between the EU countries has strengthened the demand that purely security policy and military issues must also be able to be discussed in separate Western European forums and on European terms

[919] The limitations that apply to EPS in these areas have increased interest among Western European countries in supplementary or alternative cooperation bodies

[920] The initiatives to revitalize the Western European Union (WEU) — which includes the six original EC members and the United Kingdom — must be seen as an expression of precisely this

[921] Following a reorganization in 1984, the WEU Council of Ministers holds joint meetings between the member states' foreign and defense ministers twice a year

[922] In other words, after 30 years, the WEU is now meeting regularly again at the defense ministerial level

[923] Furthermore, cooperation at the civil service level has been expanded

[924] However, the four years from 1984 to 1988 should be considered a consolidation phase

[925] It is too early to form a clear picture of what role WEU will play in the future

[926] Some countries believe that the WEU is primarily an emergency solution pending the EPS being able to address all aspects of security policy

[927] During 1988, the main lines for WEU's activities and role in the 1990s are believed to have been drawn up

[928] During 1987, a total of four countries had expressed a desire for membership in the WEU

[929] Portugal, Spain, Greece and Turkey

[930] The WEU, for its part, put the question of enlargement on hold until the future political basis for the organization's work had been clarified

[931] The French proposal for a separate "security policy charter" was central here

[932] In October 1987, the WEU adopted a joint declaration ("Platform") on European security policy interests

[933] This assumes, among other things, that the common defense will be based on a combination of conventional and nuclear weapons

[934] A first clarification of the question of a membership expansion took place at the WEU's ministerial meeting in April

[935] Referring to Article XI of the modified Brussels Treaty, Portugal and Spain were invited to negotiations with a view to membership

[936] As key criteria, the WEU pointed out that both countries had fully committed to participating in the European unification process, that both were members of NATO, and that both had officially declared their readiness to accede to the modified Brussels Treaty

[937] Moreover, both were prepared to accept in full, without reservation, the Rome Declaration on the Revitalization of the WEU and the Security Policy Platform of October 1987, and that both would participate actively in implementing them on a practical level

[938] The "Platform on European Security Policy Interests" is a comprehensive document with politically far-reaching perspectives

[939] A separate working group worked in 1988 on the practical follow-up

[940] Behind the preparation of the document is a principled and fundamental agreement on the need to strengthen the European pillar of NATO

[941] The platform also represents the framework for a definition of what the political content of this pillar should consist of

[942] However, it must be clarified that this Hague Platform reiterates in all essential points the commitments and intentions that WEU's member states have already accepted in NATO

[943] The content can be summarized as follows

[944] The construction of an integrated Europe will remain incomplete as long as security and defense are kept out

[945] The revitalization of the WEU is a contribution to the process towards European unity

[946] Due to its geostrategic situation, Western Europe is militarily vulnerable, and military security can only be achieved in close cooperation with the allied countries in North America

[947] The Harmel Report from 1967 is still valid; military security and détente policies should complement each other

[948] The main objective of European security is to prevent war

[949] To be credible and effective, the Western strategy based on deterrence and defense must continue to be based on an appropriate mix of suitable nuclear and conventional forces

[950] The significant presence in Europe of US conventional and nuclear forces plays an irreplaceable role for the defense of Europe

[951] However, Europeans have a very important responsibility themselves, both in the conventional and nuclear defense areas

[952] Arms control and disarmament are an integral part of Western security policy and there is no alternative to it

[953] A more united Europe represents a stronger contribution to the Atlantic Alliance, will promote the European role and form the basis for a balanced partnership across the Atlantic

[954] Member States undertake to ensure that the stated will to defend each Member State at its borders is made visible to all through appropriate measures, to ensure that each country's contribution to the common defence adequately reflects its initial capabilities, and to coordinate policies in the event of crises outside Europe if they affect the security interests of the Member States

[955] With regard to arms control and disarmament, the member states commit themselves to pursuing an active policy that promotes security and contributes to stability throughout Europe

[956] The WEU does not have a military organization, and the member states themselves emphasize that they do not aim to compete with cooperation within NATO

[957] In 1987, the WEU adopted a reorganization of its secretariat, merging the three working groups in Paris, the Parliamentary Assembly Secretariat in Paris, and the Council of Ministers Secretariat in London

[958] The tasks of the three working groups in Paris until 1988 were defense and security policy issues, arms control and disarmament, and cooperation on weapons production

[959] The need and interest in increased security policy and military cooperation in Western Europe is also being promoted through channels other than the WEU

[960] For example, the military cooperation clause in the German-French treaty of 1963 has been given more concrete content

[961] In 1987, a large joint military exercise was held on West German soil with the participation of, among others, the French force

[962] Rapid Action Force

[963] In 1987, it was also decided to establish a joint defense council between the two countries, and a joint Franco-German brigade

[964] The brigade will initially be under French command, and will be stationed in West German territory

[965] Since General de Gaulle took the initiative for the independent French nuclear force, French policy has been that their nuclear weapons are primarily intended for deterrence, and that they are only for the defense of French territory

[966] In a speech on December 12, 1987, Prime Minister Jacques Chirac made an expanded interpretation of the French doctrine of deterrence, stating that France would react immediately and unreservedly if West Germany were attacked

[967] The defense of France and West Germany had to be seen as a whole, and France now had weapons at its disposal that allowed the country to affirm the European dimension of its security policy

[968] In a follow-up clarification, President Francois Mitterand nevertheless emphasized that it was the French president alone who decided when France's vital interests were threatened

[969] Decision-making authority over nuclear weapons was indivisible

[970] There is reason to follow the development of military cooperation between West Germany and France with attention as it could have significant consequences for defense cooperation in Western Europe

[971] also saw intensified military cooperation between France and the United Kingdom, both in terms of nuclear and conventional weapons

[972] The two states have agreed to jointly develop a new air-to-air missile with a nuclear warhead

[973] German-British military cooperation also seems to have entered a new phase

[974] The British have once again established their role in the forward defense of Western Europe

[975] Their 56,000 men stationed in the Federal Republic still constitute the largest Allied contribution after the American one

[976] The British largest military commitment allows for practical cooperation in several fields with the West Germans

[977] In general, the British, together with the French and West Germans, appear to be leading the further development of security policy in Western Europe

[978] A number of other EU and NATO countries have expressed interest in participating in the new dynamic that now appears to have emerged in the relationship between three of Western Europe's most important countries

[979] This may strengthen the need for the WEU as a common forum

[980] At the same time, it is important to emphasize that all WEU countries — collectively and individually — have declared that their goal is to strengthen Atlantic cooperation and create an effective European pillar within NATO

[981] The WEU is therefore not an alternative to NATO, but can become a means of achieving a better balance in Atlantic cooperation in terms of responsibilities, tasks and influence

[982] The declaration of the NATO Summit in March 1988 welcomes efforts to strengthen the European pillar of the Alliance

[983] The European member states of NATO, with the exception of France and Iceland, cooperate through the Eurogroup as a separate European forum for security and defense policy within NATO

[984] The goal is to coordinate and strengthen Western European defense efforts within NATO as a whole

[985] The Eurogroup's work takes place mainly in three areas

[986] Firstly, it provides political signals about Western European views on security and defense policy matters

[987] This normally takes place during the biannual defense ministerial meetings

[988] Secondly, the Eurogroup serves as a forum for practical cooperation in the military field

[989] The instrument in this context is the Eurogroup's many subgroups

[990] Third, it should inform both North America and Europe about the contribution of Western Europeans to the common defense

[991] The information work has been particularly directed at the United States

[992] Cooperation in the material sector between Western European countries is currently entrusted to the Independent European Programme Group (IEPG), in which France also participates

[993] The Eurogroup's activities in this sector have therefore largely ceased

[994] The IEPG is formally outside NATO, but the Eurogroup receives reports on the IEPG's work

[995] Since Norway does not participate in the EPS and WEU, cooperation through the Eurogroup and the IEPG has become all the more important for our country

[996] However, there are signs that the Eurogroup is now perceived as less central by a number of our European NATO partners

[997] The increasing research and industry cooperation through the EC and other bodies may affect the cooperation in the IEPG

[998] Such development opportunities could create significant challenges for Norway in the years ahead

[999] With our exposed strategic location, it is important for Norway to maintain close connections with the rest of Europe

[1000] Isolation and special status are always a danger for smaller countries in a vulnerable position

[1001] To counter the danger, it is an important task for Norway to emphasize the broader security policy significance of developments in the High North for Western Europe and to ensure Western European involvement in these developments

[1002] From the Norwegian side, it will be a key task during the planning period to follow developments within the EC/EPC and WEU with particular attention

[1003] Furthermore, it will be of great importance that Norway fully utilizes the opportunities for information, participation and influence that NATO cooperation, including the Eurogroup, provides

[1004] Relations between the United States and Western Europe The security of Western countries is indivisible

[1005] The importance of transatlantic relations is fundamental to Western security

[1006] Unity and cooperation are therefore key words in the relationship between Western Europe and the United States

[1007] Political consultations are an important element in the alliance relationship in this context

[1008] Through a free and open exchange of opinions, based on the right of each state to formulate its policy, the solidarity that is the basis of the alliance community is continued

[1009] The development of superpower dialogue and cooperation in Western Europe has led to greater recognition of the responsibility of Western European states for their own security and political independence

[1010] But the European alliance countries fully recognize the fundamental prerequisite for their security that lies in cooperation with the North American allies

[1011] The increasing cooperation in the security and defense field between the Western European Allies therefore has as a declared objective to strengthen the European pillar of the Alliance and thus the Alliance as a whole

[1012] The United States views such a development positively, particularly to the extent that it results in a better distribution of defense burdens, in the American view

[1013] Despite the significant overall contributions of Western European countries to the common defense, criticism of the European defense effort has been raised by some quarters in the US Congress

[1014] As an extension of this, there have also been calls for reductions in the American military presence in Europe

[1015] The criticism directed at Europeans and the proposals to reduce the US military presence in Europe must be seen against the background of a number of factors

[1016] To some extent, this is an information problem

[1017] The Europeans' own efforts and role in the defense of Western Europe are far more extensive than many of their American critics acknowledge

[1018] But behind the tendency to consider Europe less important to the United States than before, there may also be a holistic global perspective, in which the Pacific region plays an increasingly important role, and in which developments in Central and South America may increasingly occupy the United States' attention

[1019] Parallel to such a worldview, where conflicts in the Third World may generally appear as more pressing threats to US interests than the likely developments in Europe, is the notion that the post-war period as a historical era is becoming a past stage

[1020] This is also where the political and psychological impact of the Vietnam War comes into play

[1021] The general picture outlined here is further reinforced by the fact that the demographic, economic and thus also the political center of gravity in the United States is moving further south and west at the expense of the traditionally more Europe-oriented east coast

[1022] Although there is a great deal of uncertainty about what specific long-term effects this will have on American security and defense policy, it seems clear that the United States is emphasizing a comprehensive global security policy that can be adapted to developments that require increased flexibility in terms of deployment options

[1023] The commission report "Discriminate Deterrence" presented in Washington in January 1988 must be considered in such a perspective

[1024] For the foreseeable future, the United States will view its involvement in Europe as a necessary security measure

[1025] However, the burden distribution may change in the future

[1026] The Atlantic Pact is based on a comprehensive community of interests and values

[1027] NATO countries need each other to protect their national interests and fundamental values

[1028] As long as both sides of the Atlantic largely share a common view of security policy challenges and have the same view of the necessity of active American participation to ensure the military balance in Europe, the most important prerequisites for the continuation of transatlantic cooperation will be present

[1029] It is difficult to imagine that responsible governments on both sides of the Atlantic will not do their part to ensure that the Atlantic partnership continues

[1030] This is necessary to ensure equilibrium in Europe and to move the Warsaw Pact member states to show restraint and negotiate how the equilibrium can be ensured at the lowest possible level of force

[1031] The uncertainty regarding developments in the years ahead lies primarily in the forms that cooperation will take

[1032] The adaptation and relative redistribution of responsibilities and tasks that may take place will also affect Norway

[1033] Main features of the military situation between NATO and the Warsaw Pact

[1034] Nuclear forces

[1035] Strategic nuclear forces

[1036] In the negotiations on reductions in strategic nuclear weapons (START), strategic weapons systems are defined as weapons with nuclear warheads and that have an intercontinental range, which for land-based missiles means over 5,500 km

[1037] There are currently several categories of strategic nuclear weapons

[1038] The main categories are ballistic missiles, long-range bombers, and cruise missiles

[1039] Rockets and missiles can be launched from the ground, from aircraft and from vessels

[1040] We are talking about a triad of strategic forces: land, air and sea-based

[1041] The different weapon categories have different characteristics and deterrent functions

[1042] The characteristics of the weapons vary in terms of readiness, survivability, flexibility in target selection, accuracy, and ability to penetrate the opponent's defense systems

[1043] The different characteristics mean that the individual categories complement each other and must be considered in context

[1044] A weapon-by-weapon strength comparison can therefore easily give a distorted impression of the balance of power

[1045] The Soviet Union and the United States have placed different emphasis on the individual legs of the strategic triad

[1046] For example, Soviet land-based intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) account for well over half of the country's strategic delivery assets

[1047] Over half of the Soviet Union's strategic nuclear weapons are located on this type of missile, and measured in payload capacity – a rough measure of the missile's ability to carry warheads – ICBMs account for about 3/4 of the total Soviet capacity

[1048] The total explosive power this provides, together with the particularly high accuracy of land-based missiles, has raised concerns on the Western side, because the Soviet Union's ICBM modernizations have greatly improved the ability to knock out American ICBM silos

[1049] Also, the ongoing introduction of mobile ICBM systems, where the weapon carriers can be transported either on roads (SS-25) or on railway tracks (SS-24), could give Soviet ICBMs increased importance because they become less vulnerable

[1050] Compared to the Soviet Union, submarines and bombers play a relatively larger role than ICBMs in the US strategic force structure

[1051] For example, warheads that can be delivered by heavy bombers account for nearly half of the US weapons arsenal

[1052] The Soviet Union has correspondingly only 1/10 of its warheads attached to bombers

[1053] Compared to the Soviet SSBN force, the United States has twice as many warheads deployed on a smaller number of submarines equipped with a smaller number of sea-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs

[1054] In return, the Soviet Union has over three times as many warheads on ICBMs as the United States

[1055] It is generally assumed that the strategic balance depends, among other things, on neither party being able to trust that by striking first they can destroy such a large part of the opposing party's forces that retaliation will be reduced to a level that is acceptable to the attacker

[1056] Considering the destructive power of nuclear weapons and the large number deployed today, there is little reason to assume that any party will be able to achieve such an advantage

[1057] The ongoing Soviet strategic modernization program has otherwise included Typhoon-class submarines (which are the world's largest and equipped with SS-N-20 SLBMs), another sea-based ballistic missile (SS-N-23), a more accurate and long-range sea-based cruise missile (SS-N-21), and the Backfire bomber

[1058] This deployment continues, and at the same time new systems are under development, including a strategic bomber (BLACKJACK

[1059] In the early 1980s, the United States initiated an update program for its strategic nuclear weapons forces

[1060] Currently, the deployment phase has begun, where MX missiles with 10 warheads each have been made operational in older Minuteman silos

[1061] Congress has limited the number of such missiles to 50. The United States has initiated development of special rail cars for MX missiles

[1062] The preliminary plans include 50 missiles stationed aboard 25 trains with two missiles on each of them

[1063] The B-1B strategic bomber has been deployed

[1064] In addition, a mobile ICBM with a single warhead (Midgetman), the new strategic bomber (Advanced Technology Bomber), and a possible ballistic missile defense system, the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), are still being developed

[1065] As part of the update of US strategic forces, the United States has also, since 1983, deployed long-range sea-launched cruise missiles (SLCMs

[1066] Most of these have conventional charges, while a smaller number are equipped with nuclear weapons for use against land targets (see section

[1067] In addition, the strategic bomber (B-52) has been armed with long-range cruise missiles (ALCMs

[1068] The strategic nuclear balance between the United States and the Soviet Union: ICBM missiles and warheads (in thousands) USA / USSR SLBM missiles and warheads (in thousands) USA / USSR Strategic bombers and warheads (in thousands) USA / USSR

[1069] IISS, The Military Balance

[1070] Short-range nuclear weapons, short-range and long-range intermediate-range weapons For the sake of simplicity, such nuclear weapon systems can be defined as non-strategic nuclear weapons, or weapons with a range of less than 5,500 kilometers

[1071] They fall into four main categories

[1072] Long-range intermediate-range weapons (LRINF) with a range of up to 1,800 kilometers, short-range intermediate-range weapons (SRINF) with a range between 1,800 and 500 kilometers, short-range weapons (SNF) with a range of less than 500 kilometers, and battlefield nuclear weapons, i.e. artillery shells and anti-aircraft missiles with nuclear weapons

[1073] Within all of these categories, there is today a significant imbalance in favor of the Soviet Union

[1074] Following the Western LRINF deployments and unilateral withdrawals of nuclear weapons in the wake of the so-called double decision and the Montebello decision, the imbalance is now numerically greatest for the shortest-range weapons

[1075] In particular, the Soviet predominance in land-based missiles is significant

[1076] The overall strength ratio in terms of SNF launchers in Europe is estimated at approximately 1:16 in Soviet favor

[1077] Another important feature of the development is that the Soviet Union has built a very extensive air defense system against Western air forces

[1078] This is a problem because NATO's INF force in Europe is largely air-based

[1079] There are also fears that the Soviet side could expand this air defense system to also cover tactical rockets and missiles

[1080] On the Western side, there are currently no plans for a defense system against Soviet missiles

[1081] The existing Western European air defense against air attacks, in turn, needs updating

[1082] A third difference is that the Warsaw Pact's tactical missiles consistently have a greater range than NATO's

[1083] During the last decade before the signing of the INF Treaty in December 1987, the Soviet Union undertook a large-scale rearmament and modernization of its land-based LRINFs through the deployment of a total of 405 SS-20 missiles with a total of 1215 warheads

[1084] This modernization program, which began in 1977, was the main justification for the NATO countries' so-called double decision in December

[1085] Through the double decision, NATO countries decided to modernize their intermediate-range nuclear weapons to the extent that the Soviet Union was unwilling to limit, or preferably eliminate, its SS-20 force

[1086] In other words, a "zero-zero" solution was implicit in the double decision, in that in 1979 NATO had no LRINF missiles in Western Europe

[1087] Without an INF treaty, the planned NATO deployment in 1988 would have included a maximum of 108 PERSHING II ballistic missiles and 464 land-based cruise missiles (GLCMs) with a total of 572 warheads

[1088] Shortly before the signing of the INF Treaty, all 108 PERSHING IIs and 274 cruise missiles were deployed

[1089] Regarding SRINF, NATO withdrew a number of PERSHING

[1090] in line with the deployment of PERSHING II

[1091] When the INF Treaty was signed, NATO was therefore left with 72 land-based German SRINF missiles (with American-controlled warheads

[1092] The Soviet Union, for its part, has in recent years modernized its SS-12/22 missiles and deployed a significant number of new SS-23 missiles

[1093] Against this background, the imbalance in the parties' INF missile strength was somewhat smaller when the INF Treaty was signed than it had been ten years earlier

[1094] However, the difference had become smaller in the LRINF category, while it had increased seriously in the SRINF area

[1095] Measured in terms of the number of deployed missile warheads, the overall INF force ratio today (according to the INF Treaty) is approximately 1:4 in favor of the Soviet Union

[1096] Regarding INF aircraft, which are not covered by the agreement, both sides are in the process of updating their systems

[1097] The Soviet Union, for its part, has developed several new aircraft in recent years with medium-short SRINF range

[1098] The most important INF aircraft on the NATO side in Europe are the F-111, F-16, F-104 and TORNADO

[1099] These are aircraft with the technical capability to deliver nuclear weapons

[1100] However, a number of aircraft with technical nuclear capability are not certified for use with nuclear weapons

[1101] A purely numerical comparison of medium-short range aircraft in operational units also goes in favor of the Warsaw Pact

[1102] A major problem for a direct comparison, however, is that most NATO and Warsaw Pact tactical fighter aircraft are technically capable of delivering both nuclear and conventional weapons

[1103] The Soviet Union also possesses chemical weapons that can be delivered from such tactical aircraft

[1104] Yet the bulk of these aircraft on both sides will be assigned conventional missions, and not all of the pilots are trained to deliver nuclear weapons

[1105] Unlike NATO, the Warsaw Pact does not specify which roles are assigned to individual aircraft and aircraft types

[1106] The ability to deliver both conventional and nuclear warheads also applies to most SNF systems and battlefield nuclear weapons in NATO and the Warsaw Pact, whether short-range missiles or artillery

[1107] The Soviet Union continues to replace the FROG missile (range 70 km) with the more accurate SS-21 (120 km

[1108] The SS-21 is also deployed in East Germany and Czechoslovakia

[1109] Artillery with nuclear capability is also being further developed on both sides

[1110] NATO, for its part, has in recent years unilaterally withdrawn a large number of warheads (2,400), including a large number of battlefield nuclear weapons, including all nuclear mines

[1111] The removal of the latter is particularly important as this type of weapon could create pressure for early use

[1112] For SNF rockets, there are currently less than 100 LANCE launchers in Western Europe

[1113] Launchers for SNF missiles can be reloaded and the total number of missiles is therefore greater than the number of launchers

[1114] In many strength comparisons of SNF missile systems, launchers are used as the counting unit

[1115] The Western withdrawal is due, among other things, to an expressed desire to avoid the misinterpretation that nuclear weapons are combat weapons to win a war, rather than deterrents to prevent it, or possibly bring it to an end

[1116] In addition to the sea-based strategic systems and land-based aircraft that primarily have maritime missions, both NATO and the Warsaw Pact have other sea-based nuclear systems

[1117] These are air defense, anti-ship and anti-submarine systems, as well as sea-based cruise missiles (SLCMs

[1118] For sea-based cruise missiles, see section

[1119] France's nuclear forces

[1120] France is not integrated into NATO's military structure, and the French nuclear forces are consequently not included in the alliance's nuclear strategy

[1121] France is nevertheless a member of NATO, and this gives the French military forces a special status

[1122] It may therefore be useful to have a rough overview of the French nuclear forces as well

[1123] The French strategic nuclear force consists of 6 nuclear-powered strategic submarines with a total of 96 ballistic missiles (SLBMs

[1124] ground-based ballistic missiles

[1125] SSBS) and 30 Mirage IV bombers

[1126] Due to the role of the weapons (the ability to hit a number of important targets on Soviet territory), these forces are defined as strategic, even by France itself, despite their range being between 3,000 and 5,000 km

[1127] Among other nuclear weapons, France has so-called "pre-strategic nuclear weapons", which in practice means weapons with a range of up to 3,000 km

[1128] These consist of 33 ground-based ballistic missiles, 38 aircraft carrier-based fighters, as well as 30 Mirage IV and 45 Jaguar fighter-bombers

[1129] In the autumn of 1986, the French National Assembly adopted a new military defense program law for the period

[1130] In addition to a strong growth in material investments in general, an update of the strategic nuclear weapons systems is planned, especially of the strategic nuclear submarines

[1131] In addition, a new land-based strategic missile, S4, will be developed to replace the 18 older S3 missiles

[1132] The modernization program also includes the modification of 18 Mirage IV aircraft, which are already equipped with new ASMP cruise missiles

[1133] In the pre-strategic role, the Mirage III's and Jaguar are to be replaced by the Mirage 2000, also with ASMP

[1134] The Navy's 38 aircraft carrier-based fighters are being modernized accordingly

[1135] From 1992, the 33 ground-based pre-strategic ballistic missiles are to be replaced by a mobile version with a longer range

[1136] The most central focus of the new program law is the modernization of the French strategic nuclear weapons forces

[1137] In addition to a marked qualitative improvement, this program involves a doubling of the number of nuclear warheads in the French deterrent force

[1138] UK nuclear forces

[1139] Unlike the French nuclear weapons, the British nuclear forces are included in NATO's nuclear strategy

[1140] At the same time, the British strategic nuclear weapons represent an independent national force that, should the situation warrant, would be controlled by the United Kingdom alone

[1141] The British strategic nuclear force currently consists of four Resolution nuclear-powered submarines, each with 16 POLARIS ballistic missiles (SLBMs

[1142] Since 1969, one of these submarines has been patrolling on a 24-hour basis

[1143] The strategic submarines are to be replaced with four new submarines around the mid-1990s, and POLARIS will be replaced with the TRIDENT D5 SLBM

[1144] The number of missiles will remain the same, while the number of warheads will increase from

[1145] Meanwhile, the POLARIS missiles are being updated to ensure the effectiveness of the British strategic deterrent in the coming years

[1146] The strategic nuclear weapons are considered a minimum deterrent by the British side, and the aforementioned updates are considered necessary in light of the obsolescence of the current force as well as the development of the Soviet air defense and ABM defenses around Moscow in recent years

[1147] Of the possible delivery means for tactical nuclear weapons, the United Kingdom has nine squadrons of TORNADO GR1 and two squadrons of BUCCANEER attack aircraft with nuclear capability, i.e. just over 130 aircraft in total

[1148] These are based in the United Kingdom and West Germany

[1149] In addition, the British Navy also has SEA HARRIER fighter-bombers equipped with nuclear bombs and aircraft carrier-based helicopters with the ability to deliver depth charges in the anti-submarine role

[1150] The latter role is also held by the Air Force's NIMROD patrol aircraft

[1151] The UK also operates one regiment (i.e., a couple of dozen) of launchers for LANCE surface-to-surface missiles

[1152] These are deployed in West Germany and equipped with warheads supplied and controlled by the United States

[1153] The British are planning to replace their older tactical nuclear weapons, and in this context are collaborating with France on the further development of a French air-to-ground missile

[1154] The conventional balance of power

[1155] Background for strength comparisons

[1156] An overall and purely quantitative measurement of the conventional balance of forces has value in itself, but makes more sense when one also takes into account how the forces can be used

[1157] Such more "qualitative" factors include everything from the parties' military-political and military doctrines, operational plans and exercise patterns to the composition, organization, geographical deployment and mobility of the forces

[1158] The latter is determined not least by geographical conditions, topography and distances, where factors such as infrastructure and supply support will be decisive

[1159] For reasons of stability, it is of fundamental importance that neither party has a force potential that equals or exceeds the minimum in relation to the opposing party's forces, which is necessary to attack and occupy territory

[1160] In other words, it is the potential invasion ability that is the focus of attention in strength comparison studies

[1161] NATO's force potential is far below this minimum, both when considering the various factors individually and in total

[1162] Moreover, NATO has neither plans for, nor desire for, anything other than being able to respond to, and repel, an attack

[1163] In order to assess possible uses for the Warsaw Pact forces, one must, in addition to their numerical superiority, also consider how the above-mentioned more qualitative factors can be thought to reinforce, or limit, this superiority

[1164] A natural starting point for such an analysis would be the organization of the Soviet forces into geographically divided strategic theaters of operations, TVDs (Teatr Voyennykh Deystviy

[1165] The Soviets have divided Western Europe into three such

[1166] the northwestern, western and southwestern TVD

[1167] A TVD can be considered a geographical area for all military operations on both own and enemy territory

[1168] A TVD includes everything from the front divisions to rear reinforcement forces

[1169] The TVD concept facilitates coordination when using forces from different branches of the armed forces

[1170] The strategic depth and breadth of the TVD will be a key benchmark in calculating the balance of power, and thus also the operational minimum for attack and occupation, within the TVD

[1171] It is further assumed that Soviet planning is based on a more precisely defined number of potential main attack axes within a TVD

[1172] Based on the main strategic objectives, these axes of attack aim to achieve specific, preliminary sub-objectives, i.e. selected parts of the TVDet that are considered important to conquer in the first phase of an attack

[1173] Just as important as the overall strength ratio between east and west is the operational strength ratio on these sections of the overall front within TVDet

[1174] Both geographical and military factors will be fundamental in the assessment

[1175] Firstly, one must take into account the quantitative balance of power within such an axis in peacetime

[1176] Secondly, it will be crucial how quickly the parties can upgrade a peacetime configuration to a wartime force

[1177] The ability to mobilize forces will be a third factor

[1178] It is likely that the Warsaw Pact will eventually concentrate its forces from the entire front on the selected axes, while on other front sections only sufficient forces will be retained to prevent a counterattack from the west

[1179] Fourth, the parties' relative ability to constantly bring forward new forces to reinforce the relevant front sections could be decisive

[1180] In other words, the local balance of power within the axis will be able to change over time, depending on what the parties can mobilize further back, how long this takes, and how long it takes to advance these forces

[1181] The latter will be determined by geographical conditions as well as infrastructure conditions and supply support opportunities

[1182] The longer the war lasts, i.e. the greater the endurance of both parties, the more important the ability to constantly bring in reinforcements becomes

[1183] Provided that the defender has a sufficient degree of endurance, the operational minimum for an attack will also have to include the balance of forces in all phases of the war's development

[1184] In addition to the above factors, the parties' ability to attack in depth, i.e. behind the opponent's main defense line, must also be taken into account in the assessment

[1185] We know that the Soviet Union has, among other things, developed the concept of so-called Operational Maneuver Groups (OMGs) for this purpose

[1186] These units are planned to be deployed very early in a major offensive and, with the support of aircraft, helicopters and airborne forces, penetrate deep into the enemy's territory to create confusion, and take out and cover key targets

[1187] Such targets may include nuclear weapons system storage facilities, airfields, air defense units, artillery concentrations, central command and control systems, communications hubs, and supply units

[1188] If this is successful, the OMGs will be able to significantly reduce the opponent's freedom of maneuver and tie up his reserves at an early stage

[1189] An operational maneuver group is not a regular organization with a fixed structure, but rather a concept for the use of selected military forces, a combat force of varying size and composition for independent operations

[1190] It is therefore difficult to say exactly what OMGs will consist of

[1191] The OMGs will be activated in war, and the situation and tasks will determine their composition

[1192] However, it is known that the groups will be organized as a combined force consisting of several types of weapons, which will also ensure the greatest possible degree of flexibility

[1193] The forces that form the OMGs will be taken from either the 1st or 2nd attack wave within the army or front that establishes the OMG

[1194] The organization of Soviet forces in TVDs, the possibility of concentration of forces within each TVD in main attack axes, the Soviet Union's very significant ability to constantly advance reinforcements within these axes due to the mobility of the forces and the country's mobilization potential and well-developed delivery system, as well as the concept of early attacks in depth are all factors that complicate the assessment of the conventional balance of power between East and West, and thus of how stable this balance is today

[1195] A review of the most important factors that will affect a potential crisis situation, however, shows that operational conditions locally and over time can be just as decisive as the overall balance of power between the alliances

[1196] An overall balance of forces that, in isolation, would not indicate the possibility of attack, can be changed locally, and in a short time, to a very significant preponderance in favor of the Warsaw Pact

[1197] Such a local concentration of forces could provide the necessary breakthroughs in relation to NATO's forward defense lines and tear them apart so that they would no longer be able to conduct a coherent conventional defense

[1198] A comparison of the conventional balance of power between East and West must take into account that the forces have different roles and reflect different traditions

[1199] They are therefore differently composed

[1200] The different geographical situation of the two sides also plays a role

[1201] One problem, for example, is how far to go when it comes to including Soviet forces furthest east and south towards the Urals and the Caucasus, or NATO forces in the United States earmarked for operations in Europe

[1202] In addition, several uncertainties related to the quality of weapons, the morale of the forces, training standards, the effectiveness of the management apparatus, tactics and strategy, as well as political will and cohesion within each of the alliances are difficult to quantify

[1203] Such factors also contribute to making work on balanced armament reductions more difficult

[1204] For a more comprehensive account of problems related to quantitative and qualitative force assessment, see St. meld. no. 58 (1986-87), On security and disarmament

[1205] The geostrategic asymmetry between East and West

[1206] NATO member countries

[1207] Atlantic Ocean (6000 km), Norwegian Sea (800 km

[1208] Member countries of the Warsaw Pact

[1209] Western studies show that the balance of power for conventional weapons has developed further in favor of the Warsaw Pact in recent years

[1210] Furthermore, the Soviet Union has acquired new weapons systems to a greater extent than NATO countries without simultaneously abolishing older systems

[1211] This trend has become apparent within all branches of arms

[1267] Nuclear weapons

[1268] The most important limitations on the build-up of the superpowers' strategic nuclear arsenals are found in the SALT agreements (SALT = Strategic Arms Limitation Talks) of

[1269] In addition, the ABM Treaty (ABM = Anti-Ballistic Missiles) of 1972 limits the parties' ability to deploy defense systems against ballistic missiles

[1270] The ABM Treaty was part of the SALT-I agreement, which also contained an interim agreement that set a ceiling on the number of intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs and SLBMs) each of the superpowers could have, corresponding to the number they had at their disposal

[1271] The interim agreement had a duration of five years

[1272] The ABM Treaty, which entered into force at the same time, is not time-limited, however

[1273] However, either party can terminate it after six months' notice

[1274] The aim of the treaty was to prevent strategic stability from being shaken by one or both parties developing and deploying extensive anti-missile systems

[1275] The agreement allows the parties to deploy one stationary, ground-based ABM system to defend a smaller area – either the national capital or an ICBM base complex

[1276] The Soviet Union has chosen to place its ABM system in Moscow

[1277] The system has recently been modernized and streamlined

[1278] The United States first deployed an ABM system at a Minuteman ICBM base in North Dakota, but later chose to dismantle it, and has not subsequently used the option to deploy a ground-based anti-missile system

[1280] The Soviet Union is also exploring such possibilities

[1282] However, the treaty prohibits the development, testing and deployment of sea-based, air-based, space-based and mobile land-based ABM systems

[1284] The Soviet Union initially thinks no, but has nevertheless suggested that the issue can be discussed further (see

[1287] However, the United States has, for the time being, made a political commitment to follow a restrictive interpretation of the agreement that does not make exceptions for ABM systems based on new physical principles and technologies

[1288] A changed American understanding and compliance with this commitment will have to be cleared with Congress and will also only occur after consultations with America's NATO allies

The INF Treaty, which was signed by President Reagan and General Secretary Gorbachev in Washington on 8 December 1987 and which entered into force after the summit on 29 May - 2 June 1988, represents a historic milestone in East/West relations and in the work towards mutual disarmament

[1311] In short, the agreement requires the two parties to remove all their nuclear land-based intermediate-range missiles, i.e. weapons with a range between 500 and 5,500 kilometers

[1312] This concerns nearly 1,300 deployed missiles (with over 2,000 warheads) and a total of over 2,500 missiles (with approximately 4,000 warheads

[1313] The phase-out will take place within three years after the agreement enters into force

[1314] In connection with a number of issues that arose during the ratification debate in the US Senate, in May 1988 the US and the Soviet Union agreed on 11 points regarding the implementation of the inspection regime under the INF Treaty, and exchanged notes confirming that the treaty also prohibits the future deployment of intermediate-range missiles with warheads based on new technical principles

[1315] Subsequently, on May 27, 1988, the US Senate approved ratification of the agreement

[1316] The INF Treaty is an important victory for the goals that were important to Norway when we advocated for the dual decision

[1317] There were two overarching goals

[1318] Firstly, to prevent a new expansion of the arms race with further deployment of nuclear weapons in Europe

[1319] Secondly, to prevent the political balance in Europe from being weakened by the build-up of a continental Soviet missile threat under the cover of the parity of strategic forces that the United States and the Soviet Union formalized through the SALT II agreement

[1320] Implementation of the agreement involves the removal of an entire category of weapons that particularly threatened the balance in Europe

[1321] This strengthens general and common security, and in particular the position of the non-nuclear weapons powers

[1322] It is true that only a fraction of the world's nuclear weapons will be removed, but all countries in Europe benefit from the removal of a significant number of weapons that can only threaten them

[1323] Equally important is that new intermediate-range missiles cannot be deployed to replace those that are now being removed

[1324] In this way, the agreement will prevent the extensive deployment of intermediate-range missiles with shorter ranges that were planned on the eastern side

[1325] It will also help halt the development of the missile that would succeed the SS

[1326] In assessing the effects of the INF Treaty, there is reason to emphasize that it is based on a number of principles that are important for future negotiations and agreements

[1327] The INF Treaty is based on asymmetrical, or unequal reductions, to achieve equal levels of force

[1328] This is an important principle with regard to negotiations on the reduction of conventional forces

[1329] The agreement further builds on the principle of comprehensive reductions rather than approving a high level of force

[1330] Finally, the agreement requires extensive control, including on-site inspection, to verify the agreement

[1331] In this area too, the INF Treaty is an important breakthrough that could have a major impact on the prospects of reaching new agreements between the United States and the Soviet Union on disarmament and arms control

[1332] The agreement also shows that the two superpowers can negotiate nuclear weapons in a way that protects the interests of Europeans

[1333] The European NATO countries that were behind the double decision in 1979 are united behind the INF Treaty

[1334] Military Security and Confidence-Building Measures (CSBMs

[1335] The purpose of the confidence-building measures that have been designed within the framework of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE) is to prevent normal military activities in peacetime from causing fear, tension and misunderstanding

[1336] The measures do not affect the military balance of power between the states, nor do they place restrictions on the scope and level of armaments and forces

[1337] The intention, however, is to enable states to distinguish actions that may have hostile intent from normal military activities, thereby contributing to increased stability and predictability

[1338] In the longer term, it is hoped that increased openness and mutual transparency can pave the way for more comprehensive limitations and conventional disarmament

[1339] The CSCE Final Act of 1975 included a first generation of confidence-building measures

[1340] The states made a political commitment through the Final Act to notify each other at least 21 days in advance of major land-based exercises in all European countries involving more than 25,000 men

[1341] In the case of the Soviet Union, the duty to notify was indeed limited to a belt of 250 km from the country's western border

[1342] On a voluntary basis, the Final Act also allowed for notification of smaller exercises

[1343] This has been done, including from the Norwegian side

[1344] The Final Act also contains a provision on the exchange of observers at military exercises

[1345] This too would be done on a voluntary basis

[1346] During the CSCE follow-up meeting in Madrid (1980-83), agreement was reached on the mandate for a Conference on Disarmament in Europe (CDE), where the parties would discuss a new generation of confidence-building measures

[1347] The conference began in Stockholm in January

[1348] In September 1986, a final document was adopted that, among other things, contained provisions on a new generation of confidence- and security-building measures (CSBMs

[1349] The new measures apply to all of Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals, and represent progress in several respects compared to the measures built into the CSCE Final Act

[1350] The deadline for advance notification of military exercises has been extended from 21 to 42 days

[1351] The notification threshold has been reduced from 25,000 to 13,000 men for land-based force formations, while independent amphibious exercises and independent parachute exercises with the participation of more than 3,000 men must also be notified (42 days in advance

[1352] Invitation of observers has been made mandatory for exercises of land-based force formations with the participation of more than 17,000 men, and for independent amphibious/parachute exercises where the participation exceeds 5,000 men

[1353] At the end of each calendar year, annual calendars of activities subject to notification in the following year shall be exchanged

[1354] For certain major activities, notification in the annual calendar must be made two years before the activity takes place

[1355] The Stockholm Document is also the first East/West agreement to establish the right to mandatory on-site inspection upon request

[1356] This is a breakthrough of great fundamental importance, also for other disarmament and arms control negotiations

[1357] A number of inspections have been carried out in both WP and NATO countries since the agreement entered into force in January

[1358] The inspection scheme is increasingly perceived as a routine confidence-building measure

[1359] It was a historic event nonetheless when Norway was subjected to a Soviet inspection for the first time in connection with the NATO exercise Arrowhead Express, which took place in northern Norway in mid-March

[1360] This inspection was considered successful

[1361] The Stockholm Document also contains a confirmation of the principle of non-use of force

[1408] Developments in the negotiating situation regarding nuclear weapons have raised the issue of the conventional balance of power in Europe

[1410] The main problems have been the question of the numerical basis for the reductions, and verification and control issues

[1411] The negotiations were fairly deadlocked in the first months of

[1412] The Soviet and Eastern European sides have previously floated ideas about a symbolic conclusion to the discussions

[1415] During the NATO Foreign Ministers' meeting in Halifax in the spring of 1986, a high-level working group was established for conventional arms control in Europe

[1434] Multilateral disarmament negotiations in the UN context

[1435] The UN Charter gives the UN General Assembly a central role as a permanent forum for addressing international disarmament and arms control issues

[1436] The UN's involvement in these issues is nevertheless mainly of an advisory nature

[1437] The UN does not make binding decisions in the field of disarmament, but adopts resolutions with recommendations to member states, or other bodies, such as the permanent Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, which is the only multilateral forum for negotiations on disarmament at the global level

[1438] The Conference on Disarmament is an independent negotiating forum in relation to the UN, but reports to the UN General Assembly

[1439] Important issues on the Conference on Disarmament's agenda include, in particular, the prohibition of chemical weapons, the cessation of nuclear testing, the prevention of an arms race in outer space, and the prohibition of radiological weapons

[1440] Norway's objectives and contribution to international détente

[1441] There is agreement on the Norwegian side that work on arms control and disarmament must be an integrated part of security policy

[1442] This was expressed, among other things, through St report no. 69 (1976-77) on the work for arms control and disarmament, St report no. 101 (1981-82) on security and disarmament, Recommendation S no. 225 (1983-84) and St report no

[1443] In this context, a number of key objectives for Norwegian efforts in this field have also been outlined

[1444] These objectives largely reflect the very definition of the term arms control

[1445] It is stated that the Norwegian side aims to create and maintain balance and stability at the lowest possible level of strength

[1446] In addition, efforts will be made to achieve greater mutual transparency in the states' military activities

[1447] The aim is also to reduce the possibility that accidents, miscalculations or technical failures could lead to the outbreak of war

[1448] In this context, a number of main principles have been emphasized, to which the Norwegian side should place particular emphasis

[1449] It is emphasized that agreements on arms control and disarmament must be concrete and lead to real reductions in military forces

[1450] Declarations of intent are not sufficient

[1451] The agreements must also be based on reciprocity in terms of respect for the parties' security situation, and equal treatment in terms of rights and obligations

[1452] Finally, compliance with agreements must be verifiable in a reassuring manner

[1453] The NST negotiations Norway's interests in the negotiations on strategic nuclear weapons are related to Norway's strategic and geographical position

[1454] Due to Norway's exposed location, an intensification of the strategic competition between the Soviet Union and the United States will also affect Norway

[1455] The government believes that a goal of the Geneva negotiations must be to prevent an arms race in outer space, achieve significant reductions in nuclear arsenals and strengthen strategic stability

[1456] The Norwegian side emphasizes that the negotiations are conducted with the aim of banning space weapons

[1457] Norway has therefore not been able to support space defense programs aimed at deployment in outer space

[1458] The ABM Treaty must be respected and enforced on the basis of a strict interpretation of the provisions on limitations on the development and testing of space weapons systems

[1459] Norway agrees with the goal of halving the number of strategic nuclear weapons as a first step

[1460] A strategic arms reduction agreement is both important in itself and important for protecting the INF Treaty

[1461] This must not be undermined by directing strategic missiles at the same targets that were previously threatened by intermediate-range missiles

[1462] The Soviet Union and the SS-24 and SS-25 programs present a particular risk of this happening

[1463] A START agreement with deep cuts in the parties' offensive arsenals would reduce the danger of "superfluous" Soviet missiles being aimed at targets in Western Europe

[1557] Main features of naval development

[1558] The Soviet Navy was for a long time a distinctly coastal navy that posed no real challenge to the Allied naval forces on the high seas

[1559] The Soviet Union had indeed built up a submarine force from the 1920s that was larger than the German one at the outbreak of the Second World War, but it was far from playing a comparable role

[1560] The development of the Soviet submarine forces continued in the post-war period, but in the first decades after the war, Allied naval forces, not least British, were also dominant in the northern sea areas

[1561] From the beginning of the 1960s, this picture began to change

[1562] The introduction of strategic nuclear-armed submarines from around 1960 represented a new element in the development of forces between the blocs

[1563] It placed new demands on strategic thinking and naval strategy

[1564] The first generations of strategic submarines, due to the relatively short range of their weapons, needed to have their patrol areas close to the opponent's territory

[1565] While Western submarine-based missiles could reach Soviet targets from positions in forward areas in the western Norwegian Sea and in the Mediterranean, the Soviet submarines had to pass out through the Norwegian Sea to reach their operational areas in the Atlantic

[1566] Soviet access to the world's oceans could best be secured from bases on the Kola Peninsula, and the Northern Fleet eventually became the most significant of the Soviet Union's four fleets

[1567] Access was central to Soviet efforts to develop and maintain the capability for strategic retaliation, and thus also to nuclear strategy as a whole

[1568] As a result of this development, Soviet interest in military use of the Norwegian Sea increased

[1569] The Soviet Union abandoned a coastal navy concept quite early after World War II and, with some interruptions, implemented an ambitious development program for an ocean-going navy

[1570] This has gradually turned the Soviet Union into a naval superpower

[1571] The justification for this changed policy can be sought in several circumstances

[1572] The Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 was a clear indication of the Soviet Union's inability to advance military-political goals outside the country's immediate sphere of influence, and contributed to an increased recognition that naval power constitutes an essential element in the struggle for influence in various parts of the world

[1573] With the flexibility that a comprehensive naval force provides, it is easier to maintain the role as a superpower in the international arena

[1574] The expansion of naval capacity must also be seen in the context of the need for protection for strategic submarines to reach their forward deployment areas

[1575] Gradually, the range of strategic submarine-based missiles was increased, and the need for patrolling in forward areas was reduced as a result

[1576] This made it possible to free up resources from the protection role for other prioritized tasks

[1577] One such task would be to prevent, or delay, Allied sea transport across the Atlantic in a crisis situation

[1578] At the same time as the build-up of the Soviet Navy took place, a tendency in the opposite direction was evident in the Western naval forces

[1579] Older vessels were scrapped without being replaced with new ones

[1580] The US Navy in 1970 consisted of around 1,000 larger vessels

[1581] This number had dropped to under 500 by 1981, at the same time as the number of aircraft carriers had been reduced from 23 to

[1582] The number of vessels in the British Navy has decreased by around two-thirds from 1949 to the present

[1583] In parallel with this development, however, strategic submarines gradually took over the role that aircraft carriers had previously played in American nuclear strategy

[1584] This led to a reduction in the need for the presence of surface vessels

[1585] Another factor was that a larger part of Western warning, control and surveillance tasks were handled by land-based aircraft and submarine forces, and by underwater-based listening and detection systems

[1586] This also led to a decrease in the presence of Allied surface forces in the northern sea areas

[1587] Soviet maritime activities in these sea areas showed an increase during the same period, at the same time as the Northern Fleet's operational areas were gradually pushed further south and west

[1588] The balance of power in the Norwegian Sea changed in Soviet favor, with the consequences this could have for Western Europe's conventional defense capability

[1589] Alongside the submarine-based strategic weapons systems, the development of the Soviet surface navy has constituted the most significant feature of military development in the High North

[1590] The Soviet Union is in the process of building its first major aircraft carrier

[1591] Together with existing Kiev-class aircraft carriers, this could, in the longer term, give Soviet surface forces a greater radius of action

[1592] However, it remains to be seen in what role the Soviet Union will use such aircraft carriers

[1593] It seems clear that the lack of experience in operating aircraft carrier groups means that it could be several decades before these become fully operational and can solve their intended tasks in a satisfactory manner

[1594] If such aircraft carriers are added to the Northern Fleet, they could also pose a potential threat to Norwegian security interests

[1595] In general, one can say

[1596] that while the Soviet Navy has grown numerically, there has been a qualitative development that in several areas has led to a reduction in the technological lead the West has traditionally had. Supply support for surface vessels, air protection and the lack of overseas bases are still considered to be one of the Soviet Navy's most serious weaknesses for operations away from home bases

[1597] An effective supply apparatus requires support points, and places demands on supply ships and air support

[1711] The development of strategic submarines and sea-based cruise missiles - consequences for Norway's position In the strategic nuclear balance, both superpowers' submarine-based strategic ballistic missiles constitute a retaliatory capability that is an important element of mutual deterrence

[1812] Some military-strategic challenges Norway's security policy situation can be seen in light of several, partly overlapping, perspectives, which will have an impact on our position and degree of freedom of action in the coming years

[1813] Firstly, Norway is placed within a North Atlantic framework, where the task is to ensure the defense of Norwegian territory and contribute to stability and low tension in the area

[1814] In this context, the strategic interests that intersect in our immediate vicinity are mainly determined by the development of the balance of power and the composition of strategic nuclear forces and naval forces in the United States and the Soviet Union

[1815] Norway's strategic position is linked to developments in East-West relations

[1816] Norway's defense must have an Atlantic foundation because only the United States can provide the counterbalance to the Soviet Union's military strength that can ensure our freedom of action and create the conditions for mutual restraint

[1817] Secondly, Norway is located within a Western European framework, where we constitute the northwestern part together with Iceland

[1819] Furthermore, it will be important to assess the consequences for our defense structure of the closer interaction between the defense of the central section and Southern Norway

[1820] Thirdly, Norway is located within a Nordic framework, linked to the close cooperation between the Nordic states and their common goal of maintaining peace and stability in the region

[1821] This means that each of the Nordic countries takes the interests and positions of the other countries into consideration when making important decisions in security and defense policy

[1822] It is about tacit, mutual consideration
